steps.title: Defining and non-defining relative clauses
steps.html:
Two jobs. A defining clause tells you which one is meant: the device that sends the data. Remove it and the sentence no longer identifies anything. A non-defining clause adds information about something already identified: the smart meter, which reports your electricity use, was fitted in March. Remove it and the sentence still works.

Commas and pronouns. Defining clauses take no commas and may use that, which, who. Non-defining clauses take commas and never that. This one rule catches most of the errors at this level.

Leaving the pronoun out. In a defining clause, if the relative pronoun is the object, you can drop it: the password (that) they were sold with, the engineer (who) we called. If it is the subject, it must stay: the device that sends the data, never the device sends the data.

Prepositions. Everyday English puts the preposition at the end: the room that the sensor is in. Formal writing moves it forward, and then that becomes impossible: the room in which the sensor sits.

Whose, where, when. Whose shows possession, for people and things alike: a company whose servers are abroad. Where, when and why follow place, time and reason.

Two special patterns. Quantities take of which or of whom: fourteen devices, most of which…, ten engineers, none of whom…. And a non-defining which can refer to a whole clause: The doorbell has been updated once, which is the problem.

steps.title: The commonest errors at this level
steps.html:
• That after a comma: the meter, that reports…
  • Dropping a subject pronoun: the device sends the data is cheap.
  • Keeping the old pronoun as well: the device that it sends the data.
  • Who’s for whose: a company who’s servers are abroad.
  • Commas that change the claim: The engineers, who were tech-savvy, refused says all of them did.

steps.title: Text A · The night the sites went dark
steps.html:
Written for this course, from reporting on the October 2016 attack on Dyn and the UK Product Security and Telecommunications Infrastructure Act 2022.

The phrase “internet of things” describes something very ordinary: objects which contain a small computer and a wireless connection. A smoke detector that tells you which room is on fire is one. So is a smart meter, which reports your electricity use without anybody reading a dial. None of this is new technology. What changed was the price, and a house with high-speed broadband now carries around fourteen internet-connected devices, most of which its owners could not list.

The technical problems that worried engineers in the 1990s were solved years ago. The ones that matter now are about who can access what, and the clearest demonstration came on 21 October 2016. Users across the United States found that Twitter, Netflix and Reddit had become unreachable, for hours. The cause was not a hostile government. It was a flood of traffic aimed at Dyn, a company which ran part of the internet’s address system, and the flood was produced by ordinary household objects.

The software behind it, which was named Mirai after a cartoon, was not sophisticated. It simply worked through a short list of about sixty usernames and passwords — the ones that cameras, routers and recorders are sold with — and tried them on every device it could find. A camera that can be hacked from the street is worse than no camera at all, and hundreds of thousands of machines whose owners had never changed a password were quietly recruited. Anyone whose baby monitor took part in that attack is still unaware of it. The code was published online, and variants of it are still responsible for a measurable share of attacks today.

steps.title: Text B · The risk that no password fixes
steps.html:
Written for this course.

Governments have been slow, and then sudden. In April 2024 the United Kingdom became the first country to ban universal default passwords on consumer devices that connect to the internet. The law, which covers everything from doorbells to fridges, also requires manufacturers to publish a contact point for anybody who finds a fault, and it carries fines of up to ten million pounds. It is a small rule that addresses a large share of the problem, which tells you how basic the problem was. Manufacturers had known about the weakness for years and almost none of them had acted, because a device that is cheap to make and quick to install sells better than one that is difficult to break into.

The interesting risk, though, is duller than a botnet. The data any single device sends is trivial: a kettle boiled at 6.40, a light switched off at 23.10, a doorbell that nobody answered on Thursday. Put together, those readings describe a life — when the house is empty, who sleeps badly, whether anybody is ill. That pattern, which nobody ever agreed to hand over, is what the argument about privacy is actually about, and no password will fix it, because nothing in it was stolen.

Which may explain a small oddity. The users who are most tech-savvy, who understand exactly how little each individual reading contains, are often the ones with the fewest smart devices installed at home. They are not worried about being watched. They are worried about being described. Everybody else is told that the technology is convenient, which it is, and left to discover the rest — usually years later, and usually from somebody who is trying to sell them something.

steps.title: Напиши свой текст
steps.sub: Напиши ответ, затем сверься с образцом
steps.modelHtml:
A smart doorbell is a device that replaces the button beside your door with a camera, a microphone and a wireless connection. When somebody presses it, or simply walks past, the doorbell sends a short recording to a company’s servers, from which your smartphone collects it a second later. The technology, which is at least fifteen years old, only became ordinary when the price fell below the price of a good lock.

What it collects is more than the visitor. A doorbell facing the street records the people who live opposite, the delivery drivers who come daily and anybody who stops to answer a phone call. Most systems keep those clips for thirty days, which is long enough to show who was where, and when.

Who can access them is the question worth asking in the shop. The answer is normally you, the company whose servers hold the clips, anybody you have shared the app with, and, in some countries, the police on request. Add to that anybody who can hack an account that still uses the password it was sold with.

Two checks, in this order. First, ask what the doorbell does when the broadband fails: a device that stops ringing is worse than the button it replaced. Second, ask how long the clips are kept and whether that can be changed, because the setting you cannot alter is the one that will matter.
